s: A case must remain live at every stage of litigation, not just when filed.
Mootness is sometimes described as "standing set in a time frame."
The exceptions matter more than the rule.
A criminal conviction remains challengeable after the sentence is served because of its continuing legal disabilities (Sibron v. New York).
Capable of repetition, yet evading review.
The challenged action is too short in duration to be fully litigated, and there is a reasonable expectation the same complaining party will be subject to it again.
The classic example is pregnancy in Roe v. Wade; elections and short-term orders are others.

A defendant's voluntary halt to challenged conduct moots a case only if it is "absolutely clear the allegedly wrongful behavior could not reasonably be expected to recur" (Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw, 2000).
Government defendants get somewhat more benefit of the doubt, but West Virginia v. EPA (2022) and FBI v. Fikre (2024) applied the doctrine to the government.
A properly certified class retains a live controversy even if the named plaintiff's claim becomes moot (Sosna v. Iowa).
